The Aba aba (Gymnarchus niloticus) is a remarkable mormyroid fish from tropical African freshwater systems, known for its elongated, eel-like body and distinctive continuous dorsal fin. In populations from the Nile basin, sexually mature adults commonly attain a total length of 167 centimeters [Li = 167 centimeters], representing the ultimate body size this species can reach under favorable conditions. At the onset of reproductive capability, individuals typically measure around 40 centimeters [Lp = around 40 centimeters] in total length, which marks the point at which puberty is first achieved. This substantial difference in length between the size at maturity and the maximum recorded size suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth following reproductive activation, a pattern observed in many large-bodied freshwater teleosts. During the early developmental stages, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weigh approximately 0.055 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.055 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameters ranging between 3.5 and 7.9 millimeters that characterize the species' relatively large, yolky ova. This initial wet weight at birth forms the baseline from which the dramatic ontogenetic increase in body mass proceeds over the course of the fish's life.

This level of fecundity is moderate compared to many other African mormyrids, likely reflecting the energetic investment required to produce relatively large, nutrient-rich eggs that develop into well-provisioned yolk-sac larvae capable of surviving the fluctuating conditions of tropical wetlands. The reproductive strategy thus combines a modest numerical output with substantial per-offspring investment.

The embryonic and larval development of Gymnarchus niloticus proceeds rapidly under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of its environment. At a sustained temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], the incubation period from egg fertilisation to eclosion lasts approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a brief interval that is typical for tropical freshwater fish spawning during the warm season. The newly emerged prolarva is entirely lecithotrophic, subsisting on its internal yolk reserves until the mouth opens and the yolk sac is fully resorbed, at which point exogenous feeding begins. The speed of this early development is tightly coupled to temperature, and under the 32 °C [T = 32 °C] regime commonly observed in the species' shallow, vegetated spawning grounds, the transition to an actively feeding, free-swimming larva occurs within the first week of life. This rapid initial ontogeny minimizes the duration of the vulnerable yolk-sac stage, potentially reducing predation pressure during the earliest post-hatching period. The resulting age at birth value of 5 days is among the shortest reported for mormyroid fishes, reflecting the species' adaptation to warm, productive waters where food resources for first-feeding larvae are abundant.

Comparative data from other large mormyrids, such as the elephantfishes of the genus Campylomormyrus, indicate that such life spans are at the upper end of the family's range and may be linked to the species' position as an apex predator within its freshwater ecosystem.

The transition to reproductive maturity in Gymnarchus niloticus involves a considerable increase in body mass from the neonatal stage. At puberty, which coincides with a total length of 40 centimeters, the wet body weight reaches approximately 344 grams [Wwp = approximately 344 grams], representing a roughly six-thousand-fold increase from the 0.055-gram mass at hatching.
